content:
**Quick answer:** Early signs of arthritis can include persistent joint pain, stiffness, swelling, tenderness and difficulty moving a joint. These symptoms do not automatically mean arthritis. But joint pain that persists, worsens, keeps returning or interferes with normal activities should be checked. A suddenly hot, swollen or severely painful joint, especially if you feel unwell, may need urgent medical assessment. ## The pattern matters more than any single sign Joint pain has many possible causes, and there is no single feeling that means arthritis. One person first notices an aching knee when walking. Another finds their fingers unusually stiff after waking. Someone else notices swelling, or that a joint is becoming harder to move. What turns an ordinary ache into something worth investigating is the pattern: pain or stiffness that persists, keeps returning, worsens, or begins to interfere with everyday activities. Occasional aches can happen for many reasons, including activity and injury. Pain becomes more important to check when it repeatedly returns, becomes more frequent, gets progressively worse, interferes with sleep, prevents normal activities, or comes with swelling or stiffness. > **Do not self-diagnose** > > Symptoms alone cannot confirm arthritis or tell you which type you have. A healthcare professional can assess the possible cause. ## Stiffness, swelling and reduced movement Stiffness may be most noticeable first thing in the morning, after sitting for a long time, or when you start moving again after rest. Its duration and pattern can help a professional understand what is happening. Morning stiffness with osteoarthritis is often shorter-lasting, while rheumatoid arthritis can cause stiffness that lasts longer after waking or inactivity. Longer-lasting stiffness does not automatically mean rheumatoid arthritis, but it is one reason to seek assessment. Swelling deserves attention too, particularly when unexplained or persistent. A swollen joint may look larger than usual, feel tight or tender, become harder to bend, or feel warmer than the surrounding area. Reduced movement often accompanies pain and stiffness: difficulty bending your fingers, gripping objects, getting out of a chair, climbing stairs, walking your usual distance, bending a knee or hip comfortably, or moving a shoulder normally. These changes can have many causes besides arthritis, so persistent difficulties deserve assessment rather than guesswork. ## Do the early signs differ between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis? Osteoarthritis commonly causes pain and stiffness, tenderness, reduced movement and grating or crackling sensations, most often in the knees, hips and small joints of the hands. Symptoms may relate to activity and can come and go. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune inflammatory condition, and the small joints of the hands and feet are often among the first affected. Symptoms can include pain, swelling, stiffness, warmth and tenderness, sometimes in similar joints on both sides, and some people also experience fatigue or reduced energy. Prompt diagnosis matters because early treatment can help reduce the risk of worsening disease and joint damage. ## Symptoms affecting several joints, and fatigue Symptoms involving several joints are worth discussing with a healthcare professional, particularly with persistent swelling or stiffness. Persistent inflammation in the small joints of the hands or feet can need prompt specialist assessment when inflammatory arthritis is suspected. Some inflammatory types of arthritis can cause symptoms beyond the joints, including tiredness and reduced energy. Fatigue is common in many other conditions too, so persistent unexplained fatigue alongside swollen or stiff joints is worth mentioning to your GP. ## When joint pain should not be ignored Consider arranging a GP appointment if unexplained pain, swelling or stiffness does not settle, symptoms keep returning or are getting worse, pain affects your sleep, symptoms stop you doing normal activities, morning stiffness is prolonged, several joints are affected, a joint remains swollen, or your mobility is changing. You do not need to wait until symptoms become unbearable. If you are unsure how to manage symptoms safely in the meantime, a pharmacist, GP or physiotherapist can advise. > **When it is urgent** > > Seek urgent medical advice for a swollen joint that feels hot, severe pain and swelling in one joint that began suddenly, red or unusually coloured skin around a joint, a high temperature, or feeling hot, cold, shivery or generally unwell; these can have several causes, including joint infection, which needs prompt treatment. After an injury, seek emergency help for very severe pain, inability to bear weight, a joint that has moved out of place, or tingling or loss of feeling. Call 999 for severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, sudden weakness or other serious symptoms. ## What to note before your appointment A few observations can give your healthcare professional a clearer picture. You do not need a complicated pain diary. - Which joints are affected, and whether one or both sides are involved. - When symptoms started, and whether they come and go. - Any visible swelling, and when stiffness is worst. - Roughly how long morning stiffness lasts. - Activities that seem to aggravate symptoms. - Whether sleep or daily tasks are affected, and any fatigue or other symptoms at the same time.

## While you wait, and mistakes to avoid If symptoms are mild and there are no urgent warning signs, avoid repeatedly aggravating the painful joint while also avoiding complete inactivity. Gentle movement may be appropriate for some people, but it should feel manageable. Stop if pain becomes sharp, severe, unusual or does not settle, and do not start, stop or change medication without professional advice. - Assuming pain is simply getting older. Persistent pain, swelling or stiffness should not be dismissed. - Waiting until pain becomes severe. You can seek advice before symptoms become unbearable. - Diagnosing yourself from one symptom. Morning stiffness, swollen fingers or knee pain can each have several causes. - Assuming every new symptom is an arthritis flare. New or unusual symptoms need appropriate medical advice. - Avoiding movement completely because a joint hurts. Some rest may help, but prolonged inactivity is not automatically best. ## Key takeaways - Early signs can include persistent pain, stiffness, swelling, tenderness and reduced joint movement. - Joint pain does not automatically mean arthritis; different types begin differently. - Symptoms that persist, worsen, recur or interfere with everyday activities deserve medical attention. - A suddenly hot, swollen and severely painful joint needs urgent medical assessment. - A short note of your symptoms before a GP appointment can make the assessment easier. ## Frequently asked questions ### What are usually the first signs of arthritis? Joint pain, stiffness, swelling, tenderness or reduced movement can be early signs. The pattern varies between different forms of arthritis, so symptoms alone cannot confirm a diagnosis. ### Is morning stiffness a sign of arthritis? It can be. Different arthritis types produce different stiffness patterns, and longer-lasting morning stiffness is one reason to seek medical advice. ### Can arthritis start suddenly? Some forms can cause sudden symptoms. Sudden severe joint pain and swelling can also have other causes and may require urgent assessment. ### Is a hot, swollen joint serious? It can be. A hot, swollen and painful joint, particularly with fever or feeling unwell, needs urgent medical assessment because infection is one possible cause. ## A gentle next step Not every aching joint is arthritis, but persistent pain, swelling or stiffness is worth taking seriously. If you have noticed symptoms that are recurring, worsening or affecting everyday life, speak to your GP rather than trying to diagnose the cause yourself. You can also explore practical arthritis information and support from Living With Arthritis. ## Trusted UK sources - [NHS arthritis](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/arthritis/) - [NHS joint pain](https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/joint-pain/) - [NHS osteoarthritis symptoms](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/osteoarthritis/symptoms/) - [NHS rheumatoid arthritis symptoms](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/symptoms/) - [NICE rheumatoid arthritis (NG100)](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100) --- *Original version clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, 6 February 2026.
